title: Hotel booking
scopeHtml: Scope: hotel room search, date-overlap booking, pricing strategy, per-room locking.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design the core of a hotel booking system: search rooms for a date range, book one, cancel, and quote a price. A guest says "double room, 1 Dec to 3 Dec" and the system must never give the same room to two guests on overlapping nights.

Clarify first (this is what interviewers score):

  • Functional: search by room type and dates, book, cancel, price quote.
  • Rules: check-out day is free for the next guest (back-to-back stays are fine); cancelled bookings free the room.
  • Out of scope for the 45 minutes: payments, reviews, multi-hotel search.
  • Scale talk: a hotel has 50 to 500 rooms; Booking.com or MakeMyTrip have millions of rooms, but each room's calendar is still tiny. That is why the room is the natural unit to lock.

Worked example. 100 rooms, 70% occupancy, average stay 2 nights: roughly 35 check-ins per day. Tiny. The hard part is correctness under two guests clicking at once, not throughput.

Industry examples. Booking.com and Airbnb treat "inventory per room per night" as the contested resource and use a row lock or a conditional write on it. Airbnb calendars block nights exactly like the half-open date interval below.

Everyday analogy. A paper diary per room: before writing a stay in, you look at the dates already inked.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating check-out day as occupied, so back-to-back stays fail.
  • Forgetting cancelled bookings must not block the room.
  • Starting with payments and never reaching the date-overlap logic.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Room: number, type, base price.
  • Booking: id, room, guest, checkIn, checkOut (exclusive), cancelled flag.
  • Hotel: owns rooms and bookings, offers search, book, cancel, quote.
  • PricingStrategy: turns a room and dates into a price.
  • Money is a long in the smallest unit (paise), never double.

Decision gravity. Booking is a separate object (not a field on Room) because a room has many bookings over time. Reversible: yes, it is only a class split. The one-way door is later, when bookings move to a database and the overlap check must become a constraint.

Everyday analogy. Room = the physical flat, Booking = a lease with start and end dates.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing booked dates on the Room as a set of days: works, but a range check is cleaner and cheaper.
  • Using double for money.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing arrows without multiplicity; always mark 1 and *.
  • Putting pricing logic inside Booking so you cannot change it.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Strategy for pricing. Why: peak season, weekends, loyalty discounts change often; the booking code must not. Alternative: an if/else chain in quote, which breaks the open/closed principle. Reversible: yes.
  • Half-open interval [checkIn, checkOut) for overlap: two stays overlap iff a.in < b.out && b.in < a.out. This is the single most important line in the file.
  • Soft delete (cancelled flag) instead of removing the booking: keeps history and audit.
  • Not used on purpose: Factory, Singleton. Adding patterns without a reason is a trap.

Worked example. Existing 1 to 3 Dec. New 3 to 5 Dec: 3 < 3? No, so no overlap, accepted. New 2 to 4 Dec: 2 < 3 && 1 < 4, overlap, rejected.

Industry examples. Airbnb, Google Calendar and Postgres daterange types use the same half-open convention; Postgres can even enforce it with an exclusion constraint (EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, stay WITH &&)).

Everyday analogy. Hotel check-out is 11:00 and check-in is 14:00, so the same night boundary can be shared.

Common interview traps.

  • Using <= in the overlap test and blocking back-to-back stays.
  • Naming a pattern with no reason; always say what it buys you.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable Java. Single file Main.java.

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.*;

enum RoomType { SINGLE, DOUBLE, SUITE }

interface PricingStrategy { long priceFor(Room room, LocalDate in, LocalDate out); }

class FlatPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    public long priceFor(Room r, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
        return r.basePrice * ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(in, out);
    }
}

class Room {
    final String number; final RoomType type; final long basePrice;
    Room(String n, RoomType t, long p) { number = n; type = t; basePrice = p; }
}

class Booking {
    final String id; final Room room; final String guest;
    final LocalDate checkIn, checkOut;           // checkOut is exclusive
    boolean cancelled;
    Booking(String id, Room r, String g, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
        this.id = id; room = r; guest = g; checkIn = in; checkOut = out;
    }
    boolean overlaps(LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
        return !cancelled && in.isBefore(checkOut) && checkIn.isBefore(out);
    }
}

class Hotel {
    private final List<Room> rooms = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Map<String, List<Booking>> byRoom = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Booking> byId = new HashMap<>();
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    private int seq = 0;

    Hotel(PricingStrategy p) { pricing = p; }

    void addRoom(Room r) { rooms.add(r); byRoom.put(r.number, new ArrayList<>()); }

    List<Room> search(RoomType t, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
        List<Room> free = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Room r : rooms)
            if (r.type == t && isFree(r, in, out)) free.add(r);
        return free;
    }

    private boolean isFree(Room r, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
        for (Booking b : byRoom.get(r.number)) if (b.overlaps(in, out)) return false;
        return true;
    }

    Booking book(String guest, RoomType t, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
        if (!in.isBefore(out)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad dates");
        for (Room r : rooms) {
            if (r.type == t && isFree(r, in, out)) {
                Booking b = new Booking("B" + (++seq), r, guest, in, out);
                byRoom.get(r.number).add(b); byId.put(b.id, b);
                return b;
            }
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException("no room available");
    }

    void cancel(String id) { byId.get(id).cancelled = true; }

    long quote(Booking b) { return pricing.priceFor(b.room, b.checkIn, b.checkOut); }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Hotel h = new Hotel(new FlatPricing());
        h.addRoom(new Room("101", RoomType.DOUBLE, 3000));
        LocalDate d1 = LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 1), d3 = LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 3), d5 = LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 5);
        Booking a = h.book("asha", RoomType.DOUBLE, d1, d3);
        System.out.println("A booked " + a.id + " price " + h.quote(a));
        try { h.book("ben", RoomType.DOUBLE, d1, d5); throw new AssertionError(); }
        catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("overlap rejected"); }
        Booking c = h.book("cy", RoomType.DOUBLE, d3, d5);   // back-to-back is fine
        System.out.println("back-to-back ok " + c.id);
        h.cancel(a.id);
        System.out.println("free after cancel: " + h.search(RoomType.DOUBLE, d1, d3).size());
    }
}

Core logic in Kotlin (same behaviour):

data class Room(val number: String, val type: String, val basePrice: Long)

class Booking(val id: String, val room: Room, val guest: String,
              val checkIn: java.time.LocalDate, val checkOut: java.time.LocalDate) {
    var cancelled = false
    fun overlaps(i: java.time.LocalDate, o: java.time.LocalDate) =
        !cancelled && i.isBefore(checkOut) && checkIn.isBefore(o)
}

class Hotel(private val rooms: List<Room>) {
    private val bookings = mutableListOf<Booking>()
    private var seq = 0
    fun isFree(r: Room, i: java.time.LocalDate, o: java.time.LocalDate) =
        bookings.none { it.room == r && it.overlaps(i, o) }
    fun book(guest: String, type: String, i: java.time.LocalDate, o: java.time.LocalDate): Booking {
        require(i.isBefore(o)) { "bad dates" }
        val room = rooms.firstOrNull { it.type == type && isFree(it, i, o) }
            ?: error("no room available")
        return Booking("B${++seq}", room, guest, i, o).also { bookings += it }
    }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Not validating checkIn < checkOut.
  • Returning null for failure instead of a clear exception or result type.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac -d out Main.java
java -cp out Main

Expected output:

A booked B1 price 6000
overlap rejected
back-to-back ok B2
free after cancel: 1

Cases to test: overlap, back-to-back, cancel then rebook, checkIn >= checkOut, no room of that type.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "I would test it" and naming no cases.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
The bug: two threads call book for the last room. Both run isFree, both see true, both add a booking. This is a classic check-then-act race.

Fix 1, simple and correct: one lock per hotel.

synchronized Booking book(String guest, RoomType t, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) { /* same body */ }

Fine for a single hotel (35 check-ins a day). Fix 2, scalable: lock per room. Keep a ReentrantLock per room, pick candidate rooms, lock one, re-check isFree, insert, unlock. Reads (search) can be lock-free over a CopyOnWriteArrayList per room since bookings are few.

class Room { final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); /* ... */ }

Booking book(String guest, RoomType t, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
    for (Room r : rooms) {
        if (r.type != t) continue;
        r.lock.lock();
        try {
            if (isFree(r, in, out)) {            // re-check inside the lock
                Booking b = new Booking(nextId(), r, guest, in, out);
                byRoom.get(r.number).add(b);     // CopyOnWriteArrayList
                return b;
            }
        } finally { r.lock.unlock(); }
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("no room available");
}

Production version (gravity: one-way door). In a real database the guarantee lives in the DB: a unique or exclusion constraint on (room, dates), or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the room row. In-memory locks do not survive multiple app servers. Booking.com style systems use optimistic concurrency: insert, and if the constraint fails, retry with another room.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking only the check or only the insert, not both together.
  • Using in-JVM locks and claiming it works across servers.
  • Holding a lock while calling payment (slow I/O).

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Add dynamic pricing (weekend +20%): new PricingStrategy, no change to Hotel.
  • Hold a room for 10 minutes while paying: a HELD status with expiry, swept by a timer (see P20).
  • Multiple hotels and search by city: add an index by city; per-hotel locks stay.
  • Overbooking (airlines and hotels do this on purpose): allow count < capacity + n.
  • Cancellation policy and refunds: another Strategy.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding every follow-up to the first design; add only when asked.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• The core rule is the half-open overlap test a.in < b.out && b.in < a.out.
  • Strategy for pricing; money as long; soft-delete cancellations.
  • Booking is check-then-act, so it needs a lock per room (or a DB constraint in production).
  • Back-to-back stays must succeed; cancelled bookings must not block.
  • Say which part is a one-way door: moving the guarantee into the database.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide whether two stays overlap, and why does a check-out day not block the next guest?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The overlap line is the heart of every booking or calendar design; off-by-one here ships real double bookings or lost revenue.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I model a stay as a half-open interval [checkIn, checkOut): the check-in night is occupied, the check-out day is not. Two stays overlap iff a.in < b.out && b.in < a.out. So 1 to 3 Dec and 3 to 5 Dec do not overlap (3 < 3 is false), and back-to-back stays succeed, while 2 to 4 Dec overlaps (2 < 3 && 1 < 4). Cancelled bookings are skipped.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Nights are what is sold, so the interval counts nights: 1 to 3 Dec is 2 nights (1 and 2 Dec).
  • Using <= would treat a guest leaving at 11:00 as blocking a guest arriving at 14:00 the same day.
  • Postgres daterange uses the same half-open convention and can enforce it: EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, stay WITH &&).
Existing  [1 Dec, 3 Dec)
New       [3 Dec, 5 Dec)  -> 3 < 3 false -> no overlap -> accepted
New       [2 Dec, 4 Dec)  -> 2 < 3 && 1 < 4 -> overlap -> rejected

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
boolean overlaps(LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
    return !cancelled && in.isBefore(checkOut) && checkIn.isBefore(out);
}
fun overlaps(i: LocalDate, o: LocalDate) = !cancelled && i.isBefore(checkOut) && checkIn.isBefore(o)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• <= comparisons that block back-to-back stays.
  • Forgetting to validate checkIn < checkOut.
  • Counting cancelled bookings as blockers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How many nights is 1 to 1 Dec? -> Zero: invalid; reject checkIn >= checkOut.
  2. Hourly rooms (day-use)? -> Use timestamps with the same half-open rule.
  3. How do you enforce it in a database? -> Exclusion constraint on (room, daterange).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "check if dates are within". Senior: names the half-open convention, shows the two-comparison test, and says where the DB enforces it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A booking site blocked all same-day turnovers for a weekend because of a <= and lost roughly a night of revenue per room.

questions.promptHtml: Explain each defect and write the corrected code.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fixes only the overlap test and leaves cancel and the validation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is check-out day free for the next guest? Do we keep cancelled bookings for audit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would fix before release because (1) loses revenue and (3) corrupts data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) !in.isAfter(checkOut) means in <= checkOut, i.e. inclusive end, so 3 Dec equals checkOut and counts as overlap. (2) cancel removes from byId but the booking stays in byRoom, so isFree still sees it (and the cancelled flag is never set), while hard-deleting loses history. (3) No date validation.
  4. How I'd verify: Tests: back-to-back, cancel then rebook, in == out, in > out, unknown id.
  5. Root cause: Inclusive interval, inconsistent removal, missing validation.
  6. Fix: in.isBefore(checkOut) && checkIn.isBefore(out); soft delete with cancelled = true and skip cancelled in overlaps; if (!in.isBefore(out)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad dates") at the top of book.
  7. Prevention: The five-case test list above; a property test comparing overlap against a brute-force night-by-night check.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hard delete bookings: audit and refunds need history.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cancel an unknown id? -> IllegalArgumentException or a not-found result, never a NullPointerException.
  • Cancel twice? -> Idempotent: no error, still cancelled.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where a hard-deleted cancellation made a refund impossible to audit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes one bug.
  • Hire: fixes all three with tests.
  • Strong hire: adds the brute-force property test and discusses audit and idempotent cancel.

questions.contextHtml: Revenue management asks for: +20% on Friday and Saturday nights, a 15% discount for stays of 5 or more nights, and a festival week at +50%. Currently Hotel.quote calls pricing.priceFor(room, in, out) and FlatPricing multiplies base price by number of nights. The first draft adds if branches inside Hotel.quote.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change under Open/Closed, and how do you compose several rules?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps adding if/else in quote or in Booking.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the rules stack and in which order (surge, then discount)? Is weekend pricing per night or for the whole stay? Does the quoted price freeze at booking time?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: PricingStrategy is already the seam: add new strategies, leave Hotel and Booking alone. For stacking rules, compose with a Decorator or a list of price rules.
  4. How I'd verify: Tests per rule: Fri+Sat in a 3-night stay costs base x (1 + 1.2 + 1.2); 5 nights get the discount; festival overrides.
  5. Root cause / design: WeekendSurge computes per night (for d in [in, out): base * (isFriOrSat(d) ? 1.2 : 1.0)), a LongStayDiscount decorates another strategy, and a SeasonalPricing looks up a date-range table. Money stays long paise; round once at the end.
  6. Fix (code):

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class WeekendSurge implements PricingStrategy {
    public long priceFor(Room r, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
        long total = 0;
        for (LocalDate d = in; d.isBefore(out); d = d.plusDays(1)) {
            boolean peak = d.getDayOfWeek() == DayOfWeek.FRIDAY || d.getDayOfWeek() == DayOfWeek.SATURDAY;
            total += peak ? r.basePrice * 120 / 100 : r.basePrice;
        }
        return total;
    }
}
class LongStayDiscount implements PricingStrategy {
    private final PricingStrategy inner;
    LongStayDiscount(PricingStrategy inner) { this.inner = inner; }
    public long priceFor(Room r, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
        long p = inner.priceFor(r, in, out);
        return ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(in, out) >= 5 ? p * 85 / 100 : p;
    }
}
class WeekendSurge : PricingStrategy {
    override fun priceFor(r: Room, i: LocalDate, o: LocalDate) =
        generateSequence(i) { it.plusDays(1) }.takeWhile { it < o }
            .sumOf { d -> if (d.dayOfWeek == DayOfWeek.FRIDAY || d.dayOfWeek == DayOfWeek.SATURDAY) r.basePrice * 120 / 100 else r.basePrice }
}
class LongStayDiscount(private val inner: PricingStrategy) : PricingStrategy {
    override fun priceFor(r: Room, i: LocalDate, o: LocalDate): Long {
        val p = inner.priceFor(r, i, o)
        return if (ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(i, o) >= 5) p * 85 / 100 else p
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Golden tests for each rule and for the stack; store the quoted price on the Booking so later rule changes do not alter existing reservations.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Decorator order matters (surge then discount differs from discount then surge); I would document the order. I would not use double.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rules change per hotel? -> Strategy injected per Hotel.
  • Price quoted yesterday vs price today? -> Freeze at booking, or quote with an expiry.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where a pricing rule change retroactively repriced confirmed bookings because the price was recomputed on read.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: branching in Hotel.
  • Hire: new strategies, decorator for stacking, long money.
  • Strong hire: per-night calculation, order of rules, price freezing and tests.

questions.contextHtml:
During a flash sale, 2 guests were both confirmed for room 101 on 24 Dec. A fix was attempted: the isFree method is now synchronized, and book is not. Another engineer proposes a lock per room using this code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Booking book(String guest, RoomType t, LocalDate in, LocalDate out) {
    for (Room r : rooms) {
        if (r.type != t) continue;
        if (isFree(r, in, out)) {            // synchronized method
            r.lock.lock();
            try {
                Booking b = new Booking(nextId(), r, guest, in, out);
                byRoom.get(r.number).add(b);
                return b;
            } finally { r.lock.unlock(); }
        }
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("no room available");
}
fun book(guest: String, type: String, i: LocalDate, o: LocalDate): Booking {
    for (r in rooms) {
        if (r.type != type) continue
        if (isFree(r, i, o)) {              // synchronized
            r.lock.withLock {
                val b = Booking(nextId(), r, guest, i, o)
                byRoom.getValue(r.number) += b
                return b
            }
        }
    }
    error("no room available")
}
questions.promptHtml: Is it correct? What is the right fix, and when is a hotel-wide lock enough?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, both pieces are locked." The check and the insert are in different critical sections.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many bookings per second per hotel? Is the data in memory or a DB? Is more than one app server involved?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a hotel-level synchronized on book immediately: correct and quick to ship.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Check outside, insert inside the lock: both threads pass isFree, then insert one after the other: check-then-act race, still double booking. (b) isFree iterates a plain ArrayList while another thread appends: ConcurrentModificationException. (c) Lock ordering deadlock: not here, only one lock per call.
  4. How I'd verify: Test: 20 threads, one room, same dates, assert exactly one booking; run it 1,000 times.
  5. Root cause: Check and act are not atomic.
  6. Fix: Re-check inside the lock:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
r.lock.lock();
try {
    if (isFree(r, in, out)) {                // re-check under the room lock
        Booking b = new Booking(nextId(), r, guest, in, out);
        byRoom.get(r.number).add(b);         // CopyOnWriteArrayList
        return b;
    }
} finally { r.lock.unlock(); }
r.lock.withLock {
    if (isFree(r, i, o)) {                   // re-check under the room lock
        return Booking(nextId(), r, guest, i, o).also { byRoom.getValue(r.number) += it }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: The concurrent test in CI; review rule that every check and its update share one critical section.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A hotel-level lock is enough at 35 check-ins a day; per-room locks help only when a single hotel has high contention. I would not claim JVM locks protect two app servers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Search is slow under the lock? -> Searches read without locks from CopyOnWriteArrayList; they may be slightly stale, which book rechecks.
  • Holding the lock during payment? -> Never; hold for a short critical section only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite Christmas Eve incident: two confirmation emails for one room and a fully booked hotel.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes the snippet is correct.
  • Hire: spots the gap, re-checks inside the lock.
  • Strong hire: also notes list thread-safety, lock scope, no I/O under lock, and the multi-server limit.

questions.contextHtml: Product says: "Users should not lose the room while they are paying." Payment takes 30 seconds to 5 minutes. During a sale 12,000 users per minute reach the payment page for the same 300 rooms. A prototype creates a booking immediately and never expires it. By noon, 90% of rooms show as unavailable but only 40% are paid.
questions.promptHtml: Ask your clarifying questions, then design the hold. What can go wrong?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Locks the room for the payment duration (holds a lock during I/O) or creates permanent bookings.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Hold duration (10 minutes)? One hold per user? Can the same user extend? What happens on payment webhook arriving after expiry? Is overbooking allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a sweep that cancels unpaid prototype bookings older than 10 minutes to free inventory now.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Holds never expire so abandoned carts hoard inventory: this matches 90% vs 40%. (b) Bots hold rooms (scalping). (c) Payment latency: red herring.
  4. How I'd verify: Query booking states and ages; compare hold-to-paid conversion.
  5. Root cause: No temporary state or expiry.
  6. Fix: HELD status with heldUntil: book creates HELD; payment success moves HELD to CONFIRMED atomically only if status=HELD AND heldUntil > now; expiry is lazy (overlap check ignores expired holds) plus a sweeper for cleanup and metrics. In SQL: UPDATE booking SET status='CONFIRMED' WHERE id=? AND status='HELD' AND held_until > now(); zero rows means the hold lapsed. Limit holds per user and per IP.
  7. Prevention: Metrics: hold-to-paid conversion and expired holds; test late payment webhook (refund or reconfirm if the room is still free).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Short holds protect inventory but frustrate slow payers; extend once on payment start. I would not hold a lock during payment, and would not skip the late-webhook path (money taken, no room).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Payment succeeds after expiry and the room is taken? -> Refund automatically and tell the user; or try an equivalent room.
  • 12,000 users on 300 rooms: fairness? -> A virtual waiting room limiting concurrent checkouts to about 300 to 600.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite flash sale where bots held every room for the full hold period and real users saw "sold out" for an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lock during payment.
  • Hire: HELD status with expiry and a conditional confirm.
  • Strong hire: lazy plus sweeper expiry, late webhook, per-user caps, waiting room.

questions.contextHtml: The hotel service runs on one JVM with per-room ReentrantLocks and an in-memory calendar. You must scale to 6 app servers behind a load balancer with Postgres as the source of truth, with no downtime, for 40,000 rooms across 900 hotels. Peak is 80 bookings per second. Today's data is persisted nightly, so a crash loses the day.
questions.promptHtml: What replaces the in-memory locks, and how do you migrate?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps in-JVM locks on six servers or adds a distributed lock for every request.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I extend the schema? Is eventual consistency acceptable for search? Rollback window? Which isolation level is used?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin each hotel to one server (sticky routing) as a short-term guard while the DB path is built.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) exclusion constraint (best), (b) row lock SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the room, (c) optimistic insert plus retry, (d) distributed lock service (extra moving part).
  4. How I'd verify: Concurrency test against Postgres with 50 clients booking the same room; shadow comparison of old and new decisions.
  5. Root cause / design: The guarantee must live where the data lives. Schema: booking(id, room_id, stay daterange, status) with EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, stay WITH &&) WHERE (status <> 'CANCELLED'). book inserts; a constraint violation means someone else won, so retry with another room of the same type. At 80 bookings per second a single primary is comfortable.
  6. Fix (plan): Phase 1: write bookings to Postgres in addition to memory (dual write, memory authoritative), compare. Phase 2: shift decisions to the DB with the constraint behind a flag per hotel. Phase 3: remove in-memory calendar; keep a read cache with short TTL. Reversible until step 3; the one-way door is when the DB constraint becomes the only guard.
  7. Prevention: Metrics on constraint violations (expected under contention), retry counts, p99 insert time; chaos test killing a server mid-booking.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a distributed lock for every booking: it adds latency and failure modes where the DB already offers atomicity. Optimistic insert can produce user-visible retries during a hot sale; try a few rooms before failing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Hot room type: everyone picks the same room? -> Pick candidates randomly or by lowest id with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED to spread contention.
  • Cross-DB (multi-region)? -> Keep one primary per hotel region; avoid cross-region writes per hotel.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite migration where six servers each held correct local locks and still double-booked because the locks did not know about each other.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: keeps JVM locks.
  • Hire: DB constraint or row lock, retry on conflict.
  • Strong hire: exclusion constraint, phased dual-write plan, skip-locked trick and one-way-door framing.

questions.subtopic: Why Booking is separate and money is long
questions.promptHtml: Why is Booking its own class rather than a date field on Room, and why is money a long?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Entity boundaries and money representation are two classic design smells; both reveal depth quickly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A room has many bookings over time, each with its own guest, dates and status, so booking is its own object; if it were a field on Room, I could store only one stay. Cancellation and history also need a record, not an erased field. Money is a long in the smallest unit (paise) because double cannot represent 0.1 exactly and rounding errors accumulate in totals.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Hotel 1 -> * Room 1 -> * Booking. checkOut is exclusive; cancelled is a soft-delete flag.
  • Storing booked days as a set on Room works but is bulky and awkward for ranges; a range check per booking is cleaner.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 in double; with long paise, 3000 x 2 = 6000 exactly. For percentages, use integer arithmetic (price * 120 / 100) or BigDecimal with a defined rounding mode.
Room 101
  Booking B1  [1 Dec, 3 Dec)  asha  CONFIRMED
  Booking B2  [3 Dec, 5 Dec)  cy    CONFIRMED
  Booking B3  [9 Dec,12 Dec)  ben   CANCELLED

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• double for money, or comparing money with ==.
  • Putting pricing logic into Booking, making it impossible to change.
  • Reusing a booking id after cancellation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you store the price? -> A frozen amount on Booking at confirmation time.
  2. Multiple currencies? -> A Money(amount, currency) value class; never add different currencies.
  3. Why not store just a boolean availability per room per day? -> Possible for a calendar table (and common at scale), but it needs one row per night; ranges are compact and the DB can enforce them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "booking holds dates". Senior: argues the 1-to-many relation, soft delete for audit, money as minor units, and the price freeze.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reporting job summed double prices over a month and was off by a few rupees, which finance noticed during reconciliation.

questions.contextHtml: Search was written as "for each room of the type, scan its bookings". It is fine for one hotel with 100 rooms. The company wants multi-hotel search by city: 900 hotels, 40,000 rooms, about 25 active bookings per room in the planning horizon (1M bookings), 400 searches per second at peak, p99 budget 150 ms. The revenue team also wants overbooking: 3% over capacity for popular dates, as airlines do.
questions.promptHtml: Estimate the current cost, redesign search, and describe how overbooking changes the booking rule.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Sends every search through the booking lock or ignores the 40,000 x 25 scan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is search allowed to be slightly stale? Filters (price, amenities)? Is overbooking per room type or per hotel? How are over-limit guests compensated?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache hot city and date searches for 5 to 10 seconds; run search on a read replica.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cost: a city search touches about 40 hotels x 44 rooms: about 1,800 rooms x 25 bookings = 45,000 comparisons, fine once, but at 400 qps = 18 million comparisons per second per city mix: CPU heavy but not impossible; city-wide without an index is the issue. Better: precompute availability per (room type, date) counts.
  4. How I'd verify: Profile search under production-like load; EXPLAIN on the overlap query using a GiST index.
  5. Root cause: Search recomputes availability from raw bookings every time.
  6. Fix: Maintain availability(hotel, room_type, date, free_count) updated in the booking transaction; search reads the table (rows for the requested nights), with the exact room assignment deferred to booking time. Overbooking becomes booked_count < capacity + allowance (allowance = ceil(capacity x 3%)) per type per night, while per-room overlap checks no longer apply: assign a room at check-in.
  7. Prevention: Load test, reconciliation job comparing availability counts with bookings, and a compensation policy for walked guests.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Counters can drift, so reconcile nightly; stale search can show a room that is gone, so book always re-checks. Overbooking is a business risk (walk costs); I would make the allowance a configurable policy, not a constant.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Counter update and booking insert diverge on crash? -> Do both in one DB transaction.
  • Date range of 30 nights means 30 counters? -> Yes; one UPDATE ... WHERE date >= in AND date < out and check all rows have free count.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where search recomputed availability from raw bookings and the database CPU saturated on the first holiday weekend.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no numbers, search under the lock.
  • Hire: availability table or index, stale-search trade-off, re-check at book time.
  • Strong hire: counters in the same transaction, reconciliation, overbooking as configurable policy with cost awareness.
